text: Fill in the key terms of the carnitine shuttle and the beta-oxidation spiral.
questions: Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and must be transferred to carnitine by *CPT-I/CPT-1/CPT1/CPT I:Which carnitine transferase is the rate-limiting, regulated step of fatty acid entry into mitochondria?* on the outer membrane.

CPT-I is inhibited by *malonyl-CoA:This three-carbon metabolite is both the building block of lipogenesis and the brake on oxidation.*, the first committed product of fatty acid synthesis, so synthesis and oxidation cannot run at the same time.
Each turn of the beta-oxidation spiral shortens the acyl chain by two carbons, releasing one molecule of *acetyl-CoA:What two-carbon unit is released at each cycle of the spiral?*.

Complete oxidation of palmitate (C16:0) requires seven turns of the spiral and yields about *106:Count ATP from 8 acetyl-CoA via the TCA cycle, plus 7 FADH₂ and 7 NADH, minus the 2-bond activation cost.* molecules of ATP.

Odd-chain fatty acids produce propionyl-CoA in the final cycle, which is converted to succinyl-CoA by a reaction requiring vitamin *B12/B₁₂:Which vitamin is the cofactor of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase?*.

overallFeedback.feedback: The carnitine shuttle (CPT-I → translocase → CPT-II) gates fatty acid entry into the mitochondrion; malonyl-CoA from lipogenesis inhibits CPT-I, ensuring the two opposing pathways never run together. Each β-oxidation cycle removes a two-carbon acetyl-CoA; palmitate's seven cycles yield ~106 ATP after subtracting the 2-bond activation cost. Odd-chain fatty acids produce propionyl-CoA, whose conversion to succinyl-CoA requires the B₁₂-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
